title: Haiti
capsule: Between 1792 and 1803, the territory later renamed Haiti was still nominally the French colony of Saint-Domingue, convulsed by the slave uprising that began in August 1791 and the abolition of slavery decreed by French civil commissioners in 1793-94. Former slave Toussaint Louverture rose to dominate the colony militarily and politically, defeating British and Spanish interventions, and by 1801 issued an autonomous constitution naming himself governor-for-life while nominally retaining French sovereignty. Napoleon's 1802 expedition under General Leclerc captured and deported Louverture, but yellow fever and fierce guerrilla resistance under Jean-Jacques Dessalines destroyed the French army, culminating in the rebel victory at the Battle of Vertieres on 18 November 1803 that ended French control weeks before independence was proclaimed.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. The geographic extent of the revolutionary state covered the French colony of Saint-Domingue (western Hispaniola), which is well-defined cartographically; zones of effective control shifted continuously during the military campaigns and are only approximately mapped.
